title: A generative developmental code that builds a specified functional neural circuit

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an explicit developmental instruction set that lets an experimenter specify a mammalian neural circuit's cell types, connectivity and computation in advance, then grow tissue that reproducibly meets those targets. The instructions would describe how to produce the circuit through development, rather than merely describe its final anatomy. Self-organization could be part of the process, provided its outcomes satisfy the prospective specification.

Anthony M. Zador's 2019 perspective supplies the conceptual rationale: a mammalian genome has insufficient information capacity to enumerate every synaptic connection, so it must encode rules that generate wiring during development. A compact set of rules can therefore produce a much larger circuit. Turning that argument into a usable biological construction method would require identifying sufficient instructions and showing that they reliably produce the intended connectivity and function.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would make specified functional neural tissue an object of deliberate construction. Within the demonstrated circuit class, researchers could change developmental instructions and measure the resulting changes in wiring and computation. That would enable causal tests connecting developmental rules to circuit function, extending the wiring-rule rationale in Zador's perspective into a biological engineering capability.

A successful engineered instruction set would establish a sufficient route to the tested circuit. It would not by itself show that natural genomes use the same mechanisms, that the instructions are necessary, or that arbitrary circuits can be grown. Correspondence with natural development would require additional validation. Likewise, the analogy to compiling a circuit specification is useful only if the contributions of starting cells, environmental signals, activity and training are included explicitly; the specification need not determine every individual synapse.

A conditional downstream possibility is supplying designed tissue for reconstruction after neuronal loss. Restoring a person's specific memories would require substantially more: developmental scaffolding does not specify the experience-dependent information learned on that scaffolding. Identifying and reinstating learned content, and integrating the resulting tissue appropriately into the host, would remain separate requirements.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is a sufficient developmental specification linking defined starting cells and instructions to a prospectively specified mammalian circuit and computation. Zador's perspective motivates searching for generative wiring rules, but does not provide a demonstrated biological construction protocol. The supplied evidence also does not establish the field-wide availability or absence of this capability in 2026.

Engineering synthesis: the central challenge is to turn a desired outcome into interventions that control cell identities, spatial organization, connection formation and functional maturation together. The specification would need to identify which developmental signals and activity-dependent processes are sufficient, when they must occur, and which features can be left to self-organization. It would also need to distinguish tolerable biological variation from variation that changes the intended computation. These are requirements inferred from the proposed capability, rather than a verified inventory of unresolved mechanisms.

Engineering synthesis: structural and functional sufficiency must be established separately and then linked. Recognizable anatomy, survival, maturation or host integration alone would not establish the intended computation. Conversely, a useful output alone would not establish the intended wiring. Any dependence on host circuitry, sensory input or training must be characterized so that the causal contribution of the developmental instructions can be assessed.

current_state.text: Zador's 2019 Nature Communications perspective, volume 10, article 3770, argues that genomes encode developmental wiring rules through a genomic information bottleneck. According to the supplied review of the complete perspective, it develops the conceptual argument and implications for artificial neural networks; it does not demonstrate an instruction set that grows a biological circuit to a prospective connectivity and computation target. Its distinction between innate scaffolding and learned information also limits what developmental construction alone could accomplish.

Max Kozlov's Nature news article dated 16 September 2026 reports that human brain tissue transplanted into mice lacking a cerebral cortex can grow to occupy most of the vacant space and connect with the host nervous system. The supplied review had access only to the opening preview before access options interrupted the article. That preview supports a limited report of growth and integration, but leaves prospective wiring targets, computational performance and reproducibility unassessed. Occupying a vacant region does not, by itself, demonstrate the capability defined here; the limited preview also cannot establish that the underlying experiment omitted such tests.

The research notes attribute improved maturation and the ability of transplanted human cells to drive reward-seeking in a rat to Revah and colleagues' 2022 study. They also attribute limitations in cultured organoid connectivity to that work. Those details remain unverified within this record because the study's source text and URL were not supplied. The 2026 Kaganovsky primary paper was likewise unavailable to the supplied review and appeared only through the news references. These evidence gaps limit the conclusions available here; they do not establish that the reported results are false.

The supplied materials do not establish current organoid variability, the extent to which developmental rules have been decoded, or whether some prospectively specified mammalian circuits can already be grown reproducibly. The supplied search record is empty, so completeness as of the review's 1 November 2026 cutoff remains unresolved. The dated sources therefore motivate the innovation without establishing a comprehensive account of the contemporary field.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: two independent laboratories use defined starting cells and an explicit instruction set to grow the same specified small mammalian circuit. A sensory column or corticothalamic loop could be considered as an example, although their feasibility as initial targets is not established by the supplied evidence. Both laboratories would meet preregistered structural and computational criteria. Independent replication and preregistration are proposed methodological choices, not established standards supplied by the sources.
completion_criteria.label: Two independent laboratories grow the specified circuit meeting preregistered criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurements should define the required cell types, spatial organization, wiring resolution, acceptable connectivity variation and computational performance before development begins. The protocol should specify preparation numbers, success rates and variation across preparations, with enough independent repetitions to assess reliability. Structural measurements and functional tests should jointly establish that the grown tissue meets the target, rather than relying on appearance or a selected successful specimen.
completion_criteria.label: Report circuit specification, target attainment and reliability across preparations

completion_criteria.text: The demonstration should disclose and evaluate required environmental inputs, developmental activity, training and host contributions. An organoid produced through self-organization could qualify if it met the prospective specification and reproducibility criteria; spontaneous differentiation or maturity alone would be insufficient. Any claim that engineered instructions reproduce natural genomic mechanisms would require separate evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Disclose and evaluate required developmental inputs and supporting contributions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed extensions would test whether changing instructions predictably changes connectivity and computation, and whether the method transfers across additional cell types, architectures and tasks. Such tests would establish demonstrated breadth within stated practical boundaries. A finite collection of successful circuits would not establish literal universality or unrestricted circuit programmability.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate predictable circuit changes and transfer within stated practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NEU-01, simultaneous spike-resolved recording, and NEU-02, whole-brain synaptic-resolution connectomics, concern measurement capabilities that could help assess activity and wiring. NEU-08 concerns producing a circuit. A small-circuit demonstration would require adequate measurements at its own scale, without necessarily requiring either whole-brain capability.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-03 seeks a prospective theory predicting mammalian circuit computation from connectivity. It overlaps with NEU-08's need to connect wiring targets to functional targets, but their success conditions differ. A growth protocol could empirically produce a specified circuit without providing a general predictive theory, while a predictive theory would not itself supply developmental construction instructions.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-05 addresses target-specific regrowth of long axons in the adult central nervous system, while NEU-06 addresses reconstruction of human cognitive circuits after neuronal loss. NEU-08 could contribute designed tissue or developmental guidance to those efforts. Growing a specified circuit would still leave distinct questions about adult host conditions, long-range targeting, integration and recovery of cognitive function.

NEU-04 concerns content-faithful reading and writing of specific episodic memories. Its distinction from NEU-08 follows the separation between developmental scaffolding and experience-dependent information emphasized by Zador. Reconstructing circuitry through NEU-06 and growing tissue through NEU-08 would not automatically reinstate an individual's memories; that would additionally require capabilities of the kind identified by NEU-04.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-09 concerns cell-type-specific molecular access throughout the intact adult human brain, and NEU-11 concerns reversible reopening of critical-period plasticity in selected adult circuits. Molecular targeting and plasticity control could become enabling components of some NEU-08 implementations, especially in a host. Their adult-brain scope and distinct objectives mean that a developmental construction demonstration would not establish either capability.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-07 concerns noninvasive cellular read and write through the intact adult human skull, NEU-10 a causal account of conscious content, and NEU-12 completing sleep's necessary functions without a normal sleep period. These are separate access and explanatory capabilities. Meeting NEU-08's structural and computational criteria would not establish them, nor would its proposed initial demonstration require resolving all three.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish how broadly prospective mammalian circuit construction is available as of 1 November 2026 or the later source-retrieval date.
Revah's 2022 findings remain unverified within this record because its source text and URL were not supplied.
The Kaganovsky primary paper and the full Kozlov news article are unavailable here; their detailed experimental design, results and treatment of prospective specification remain unresolved.
Current organoid variability and the extent of decoded developmental wiring rules are not established by the supplied texts.

The proposed initial circuit, wiring resolution, tolerances, preparation numbers and performance thresholds still require selection; the supplied evidence does not establish the feasibility of the suggested examples.
Whether an engineered sufficient instruction set would reproduce natural genomic mechanisms requires separate validation.

brief.title: Brain tissue grown to a chosen design
possible: Researchers could choose the cell types, connections and signal-processing task of a small brain circuit—a connected group of nerve cells—before growing it. A set of developmental instructions would then reliably produce living mammalian tissue that meets that design.
why: Researchers could change the growth instructions and measure how those changes alter connections and function. This would let them test how development shapes what a brain circuit does.

sources.who: Max Kozlov, reporting on K. Kaganovsky and colleagues
sources.showed: Kozlov reported that transplanted human brain tissue grew to fill much of the space in mice missing their cerebral cortex, an outer brain region, and connected with their nervous systems.
sources.quote: Human brain tissue transplanted into mice that lack a key part of their brains can grow to occupy most of the vacant space and wire into the animals’ nervous systems.
sources.cited_for: Human brain tissue can grow and connect within a host brain.
sources.not_established: Growth and host connections alone do not establish that tissue meets a design chosen in advance or performs its intended task.

sources.showed: Zador argued that DNA cannot list every brain connection individually. Instead, it must encode developmental rules that generate the wiring. This was a conceptual argument.
sources.cited_for: Compact developmental rules could generate a much larger brain circuit.
sources.not_established: The perspective did not demonstrate growth instructions that reliably produce a circuit with chosen connections and function.

shown: Human brain tissue has grown and connected inside mice missing their cerebral cortex. This demonstrates growth and integration with a host; meeting a circuit design chosen before growth remains a separate requirement.
missing: A demonstrated set of growth instructions must link defined starting cells to the intended cell types, arrangement, connections and function.
Repeated preparations must meet both wiring and signal-processing targets, with clear limits on acceptable variation.
The contributions of the host, environmental signals, activity and training must be measured.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories grow the same specified circuit
milestones.explanation: Two independent laboratories would grow the same small mammalian circuit and meet structural and functional criteria registered before experiments. This would establish independent repeatability.

milestones.label: Repeated preparations meet declared wiring and performance targets
milestones.explanation: Tests would measure success rates and variation against advance targets for cell types, arrangement, connections and signal processing. This would distinguish reliable construction from an isolated success.

milestones.label: Required growth conditions and supporting contributions are established
milestones.explanation: Experiments would disclose and evaluate the required environment, activity, training and host support. This would establish what the growth instructions need to produce the intended circuit.

milestones.label: Instruction changes predictably alter circuits across additional designs
milestones.explanation: Changing instructions would predictably change connections and signal processing, with transfer tested across additional cell types, layouts and tasks. This would establish the method’s practical range.

uncertain: The initial circuit, connection detail, acceptable variation and performance thresholds still need to be chosen.
It remains unclear how broadly researchers can already grow mammalian circuits to designs chosen in advance.
An engineered recipe could work without matching natural development. Growing circuitry would also not, by itself, restore someone’s learned memories.

page.title: Developmental programming of mammalian neural circuits
page.definition: A developmental instruction set repeatedly grows living mammalian neural circuits to a design chosen before growth: cell types, synaptic connections and an input–output computation. A synapse is a signalling contact between nerve cells; the instructions include required environmental cues, activity and training.

goal.need: Zador’s 2019 information-budget argument compares a human genome holding at most about 1 GB with about 3.7 × 10^15 bits needed to list the targets of roughly 10^14 synaptic connections. These estimates motivate testing whether compact developmental rules can construct specified wiring and function. NSF’s RECODE programme seeks reproducible differentiation rules leading to functional cells or organoids.

figures.caption: Zador’s illustrative information-budget comparison
rows: Explicit list of synaptic connection targets
figures.note: The connection estimate assumes about 10^11 neurons and 10^14 connections and excludes synaptic strengths. These are estimates in a conceptual argument.

statements.quote: Projects responsive to this solicitation must aim to establish a robustly validated and reproducible set of differentiation design rules
statements.context: RECODE includes nervous-system products among its eligible functional cells and organoids.

statements.quote: Achieving in vitro guidance of functional neuronal connections between CBOs via 3 dimension (3D) bioprinting
statements.context: CBOs are cortical brain organoids. This is an objective in a brain-repair project whose grant agreement was signed on 29 June 2023.

completion.title: Developmental instructions repeatedly grow mammalian circuits to a prospective wiring and computation design.
completion.criterion: For a declared mammalian circuit class, an explicit developmental rule set converts a chosen cell-type composition, connectivity pattern and input–output computation into growth instructions. Tissues grown in independent preparations meet all three prospective specifications within their predefined tolerances. Starting cells, environmental cues, activity and training are included in the instructions.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body’s published test for this combined capability was found.
completion.basis: Searches of NSF RECODE, NIH BRAIN roadmaps, organoid consensus guidance, standards and neuroscience prizes found no completion test combining prospective cell identity, wiring, computation and reproducibility. This fallback joins RECODE’s differentiation-design goal to the consensus framework’s structural and functional validation. It is restricted to a declared circuit class.

milestones.title: Human cortical spheroids express forebrain markers FOXG1 and PAX6 at about day 25.
milestones.criterion: Human cortical spheroids express FOXG1 and PAX6, markers of forebrain identity, at about day 25 under Sloan et al.’s protocol. The protocol supplies no minimum positive-cell fraction. Yoon et al., published online 20 December 2018, tested day-25 marker expression in 12 induced pluripotent stem-cell lines from 11 donors. Across 85 differentiation experiments using 12 lines, 90% maintained spheroids beyond 100 days. That percentage is a result, not an acceptance threshold.
milestones.set_by: Sloan et al., Nature Protocols, Anticipated Results; this endpoint was written for human cortical spheroids.
milestones.threshold_quote: At early stages, hCS should express the forebrain markers FOXG1 and PAX6 (e.g., day 25)

milestones.title: Cortico-striatal assembloids transmit cortical stimulation to striatal neurons.
milestones.criterion: Cortical projections form functional connections with striatal neurons. The published assay tests whether cortical stimulation evokes striatal calcium responses time-locked to stimulation, compared with responses at randomized times. Miura et al., published 3 December 2020, found higher stimulation-aligned responses in 180 cells from 10 assembloids derived from 3 induced pluripotent stem-cell lines (two-sided Wilcoxon P = 0.0002).
milestones.set_by: Miura et al., author-deposited assembloid protocol, section 48; this functional endpoint was written for human cortico-striatal assembloids.
milestones.threshold_quote: To verify whether responses are time-locked to LED stimulation, compare ΔF/F responses to ΔF/F values obtained at randomly selected time points.

milestones.title: Cortico-motor assembloids turn cortical stimulation into synaptically mediated muscle contraction.
milestones.criterion: In the cortico-motor assay, cortical activation evokes skeletal-muscle contraction through intervening hindbrain/spinal tissue; blocking excitatory synaptic transmission abolishes the evoked contraction. Andersen et al., published online 16 December 2020, found responding assembloids at 5 and 8 weeks after assembly: 81% and 50%, respectively (16 assembloids at each time point, 2 induced pluripotent stem-cell lines, 1 differentiation). These percentages are results, not acceptance cutoffs.
milestones.set_by: Andersen et al., Cell, cortico-motor functional assay and Figures 6–7; this endpoint was written for human cortico-motor assembloids.
milestones.threshold_quote: The functional output of the cortico-motor circuit is muscle contraction through motor neuron activity.

milestones.title: Developmental instructions produce a mammalian circuit meeting prospective wiring and computation targets.
milestones.criterion: A developmental rule set derived from a circuit design produces mammalian tissue meeting that design’s preselected cell-type, connectivity and quantitative input–output targets in an initial construction experiment. Target-specific tolerances and required environmental or training inputs are fixed before growth. This is the prototype stage before reproduction in independent preparations; no matching end-to-end demonstration was identified in the cited studies.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of RECODE, organoid consensus guidance and circuit-engineering protocols found no combined prospective prototype test.

not_found: No published acceptance values for wiring error, computation error, success fraction or replication count were found for developmental construction of a specified mammalian neural circuit.

results.finding: Human cortical spheroids from 12 hiPSC lines expressed FOXG1 and PAX6 at day 25.
results.detail: The paper reports transcriptional upregulation; it does not give a positive-cell fraction. The 12 lines came from 11 donors.
results.quote:
After 25 days of differentiation, hCS-FF showed strong transcriptional upregulation of
the forebrain markers FOXG1, SIX3 and PAX6, in the absence of endoderm (SOX17) and
mesoderm (BRACH) markers

results.finding: In cortico-striatal assembloids, 180 striatal cells showed higher stimulation-aligned calcium responses than at random times (P = 0.0002).
results.detail: Some cells did not respond or fired spontaneously during stimulation. Glutamate receptor antagonists blocked the light-induced responses.
results.quote: The median ΔF/F of GCaMP6 signals was significantly higher following light stimulation as compared to the median ΔF/F at randomly selected time-points

results.finding: Cortico-motor assembloids: 85.7% of 7 tested showed muscle contraction after cortical stimulation.
results.detail: At 20–30 days after assembly, contraction depended on the hindbrain/spinal spheroid; excitatory glutamate receptor blockers abolished the light-induced response. The assembloids were derived from 3 hiPS cell lines across 1–2 differentiations.
results.quote: Activation of Chrimson-expressing hCS induced global contractions in hSkM in 85.7% of tested assembloids (p = 0.01)

results.finding: Across four human cortical spheroid samples, cortical glutamatergic neurons comprised 54%–59% of cells.
results.detail: Directed differentiation produced cortical cell types, but the study did not test a prospectively specified circuit design with cell-type, connectivity and quantitative input–output targets.
results.quote:
The proportion of cortical glutamatergic neurons varied between 54% and
59% of all cells in the four hCS samples.

results.finding: In cortico-striatal assembloids, 11 of 35 recorded striatal cells responded to cortical stimulation.
results.detail: The responses indicate functional synaptic connectivity. The study does not report a prospectively specified circuit design with quantitative cell-type, connectivity and input–output targets.

results.finding: Cortico-motor assembloids: cortical stimulation induced muscle contraction in 85.7% of 7 tested assembloids.
results.detail: The assembled circuit linked cortical stimulation to muscle contraction, but the text does not establish preselected cell-type, connectivity and quantitative input–output targets with tolerances fixed before growth.
results.quote: Activation of Chrimson-expressing hCS induced global contractions in hSkM in 85.7% of tested assembloids (p = 0.01)
